title: MoE-Spec: Expert Budgeting for Efficient Speculative Decoding (McDanel, Li, Surineni, Khaitan; Meta Reality Labs / F&M; arXiv 2602.16052v1, 17 Feb 2026)
setting: OLMoE-1B-7B, Qwen3-30B-A3B (EAGLE-3 drafts), Mixtral-8x7B (EAGLE-1); A100 80GB (2 for Mixtral), FP16, all experts GPU-resident, 63-token draft trees, single request; baseline = EAGLE-3 (EAGLE-1 for Mixtral)
headline: 10-30% over EAGLE-3 (abstract); Table 1 Mixtral MBPP T=0 2.3x vs 1.7x, Qwen3 GSM8K 2.4x vs 1.9x; Sec 4.2 mean relative gain 27% Mixtral, 16% Qwen3, 6% OLMoE; acceptance length drops about 1.4%
caveat: Experts fit in HBM, no offloading, no SSD; gain is HBM-bandwidth of the union. The budget truncates routing (an approximation: Mixtral falls to about 78% of AR quality at max speedup). Authors say batched serving may give smaller gains.
notes: Truncation of verifier experts is a quality-changing approximation, not the exact union that our family #0 test models.

title: Less Experts, Faster Decoding: Cost-Aware Speculative Decoding for MoE (EcoSpec; Xie, Liu, Huang et al.; arXiv 2607.12696v1, 14 Jul 2026)
setting: DeepSeek-V3.1 671B (MTP baseline), Qwen3-235B-A22B and GPT-OSS-120B (EAGLE-3 baseline); 8x H200 (arXiv html); batch 1 main, batch 1/2/4 in Appendix A; HF Transformers prototype; no offloading stated (HBM-read analysis); small 0.6B/1.5B expert predictor, about 4 ms/step
headline: Averages over 7 benchmarks: Qwen3-235B 1.22x->1.36x (T=0), GPT-OSS-120B 1.14x->1.31x, DeepSeek-V3.1 1.10x->1.15x; peak 1.62x on MT-Bench Qwen3-235B; at batch 8 both fall below AR (0.69x / 0.65x)
caveat: 'Up to 1.62x' is a single-benchmark peak; typical gain over EAGLE-3 is +0.05 to +0.17x. 8 H200 GPUs, memory-traffic reductions are estimates from footprints, not measured. Predictor trained and tested on the same seven benchmarks.
notes: Catalog implies an offload speedup; the paper does not evaluate offloading at all.

title: DraftExpert: Expansion-Aware Self-Speculative Decoding for End-Device MoE Inference (Dengke Han; arXiv 2607.24434v1, 27 Jul 2026)
setting: DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Moonlight-16B-A3B (64 routed + 2 shared, top-6, 27 layers). CG: RTX 4090 24GB, BF16, experts in host RAM copied on demand. MN: Xiaomi phone Snapdragon 8 Elite NPU, experts in Flash, llama.cpp Q4_0. Single user. Baseline = AR with offloading
headline: Table 2 decode TPS: DS CG 2.19->2.99 (1.36x), DS MN 10.18->15.47 (1.52x), ML CG 1.94->2.50 (1.29x), ML MN 8.50->13.69 (1.61x); avg 1.45x; acceptance 83-87%, prefetch hit 86-88%; verification cost about 40% lower than fixed-length speculation. Naive 'shared+top-r' drafting is slower than AR (1.19 vs 2.19 TPS)
caveat: States (Fig 1) that a multi-token verify activates the union, so it is not one target step: supports our mechanism. Its offloaded tier is host RAM or phone Flash with a resident learned draft (extra training, extra memory), models are 16B. Not a 125B and not a laptop SSD at 8 GB.
notes: Useful as evidence that naive speculation under offload loses to AR, which is consistent with our byte-side refutation; the win needs a trained fixed-footprint drafter.

title: Accelerating MoE Inference by Hiding Offloading Latency with Speculative Decoding (SpecMoEOff; Wang et al., Nanjing Univ / HKUST; arXiv 2508.21706v1, 29 Aug 2025)
setting: Mixtral-8x7B FP16 (about 87 GB) + EAGLE draft; A30 + Xeon 6426Y 250GB RAM, and 4090D + Xeon 5418Y 190GB; global batches of 515-824 (roofline); baselines DeepSpeed-ZeRO-Inference, MoE-Lightning, itself without SD
headline: Up to 2.5x decode throughput vs MoE-Lightning (abstract); 1.6-2.9x avg 2.1x (Sec 6.2, Figs 8-9); 11.3-27.5x vs DeepSpeed; SD alone adds 1.53x (APPS) / 1.45x (CNN/DM)
caveat: Offline high-throughput regime with hundreds of sequences per batch and 190-250 GB of CPU RAM; the mechanism (more tokens per loaded expert) is the opposite of our batch-1 problem, where the extra tokens come from one sequence and add experts.
notes: Catalog 'one loaded expert serves a few inputs' understates: it needs a very large batch. Part of the 2.5x is memory management, not SD (the no-SD variant already beats MoE-Lightning). Code not mentioned as released.

title: MoE-SpeQ: Speculative Quantized Decoding with Proactive Expert Prefetching and Offloading for MoE (Wang et al., SJTU; arXiv 2511.14102v1, 18 Nov 2025) and SP-MoE (Chen et al.; arXiv 2510.10302v2, 6 Nov 2025)
setting: MoE-SpeQ: Phi-3.5-MoE 41.9B, Qwen1.5-MoE 14.3B, DeepSeek-V2-Lite 15.7B; FP16 target + INT4 GPTQ draft; one A100 40GB, Xeon 4310, 256GB RAM, PCIe4. SP-MoE: Mixtral-8x7B, Phi-3.5-MoE, DeepSeek-Lite; RTX 3090/4090/A100, 512GB-1TB RAM, batch 1, experts in host RAM
headline: MoE-SpeQ: abstract 'at most 2.34x' over the offloading framework on Phi-MoE, but Sec 4.2 gives 163.1 vs 536.7 ms/token = 3.3x on Phi-MoE (vs Mixtral-Offloading-SC); prefetch hit rate >96% (Table 3). SP-MoE: abstract 1.07-3.5x TPOT; Sec 5.1 avg 34% less TPOT than Mixtral-Offloading, 19% vs MoE-Infinity, 12% vs AdapMoE (Figs 9-10; captions say 1.35x and 2.3x)
caveat: Both stage experts from host RAM over PCIe to a GPU, not from SSD to CPU; baselines are weak/reimplemented offloaders; headline numbers inconsistent inside each paper; SP-MoE is greedy sequential drafting only (no trees). One catalog row covers two papers.
notes: SP-MoE fetched via the arXiv abstract page first (no details), then via html v2 (read). MoE-SpeQ last 8k chars not read.

title: S2-MoE: Enabling Efficient Self-Speculative Decoding for Mixture-of-Experts on Edge Devices (Huang, Qiu, Li; arXiv 2608.15018, submitted 15 Aug 2026, v2 19 Aug 2026)
setting: OLMoE-1B-7B, DeepSeek-V2-Lite-Chat, Qwen3-30B-A3B, GPT-OSS-120B (116.8B, 4 of 128 experts). Jetson Orin NX 16GB and AGX Orin 32/64GB (overflow params go to SSD); RTX 4090 with constrained memory (cold experts in CPU RAM). Built in llama.cpp. Baselines: AR, EAGLE-3 branch, expert sparsity, layer sparsity, Cascade-on-EAGLE-3. Batch not stated (edge, 1-2)
headline: Abstract: up to 5.3x over AR, about 2.0x average; Jetson 1.3-5.3x, RTX 4090 1.2-2.9x; e.g. Orin NX 16GB OLMoE HumanEval 5.25x, DeepSeek HumanEval 3.76x (Appendix Tables 5-8). Reuse-aware gating biases routing: PPL ratio about 1.012-1.013, top-1 agreement >89%
caveat: Catalog says numbers unread; now read: this is the closest published setting to ours (llama.cpp, SSD tier, tight memory, batch 1). Speedups grow as memory gets tighter. But baseline is AR with the same offload (not an LRU-cache-tuned best path), models are small (largest GPT-OSS-120B fits in 64GB), the gating is lossy (bounded routing bias), and the Jetson's SSD/UMA differs from a laptop CPU.
notes: Page text read to 100k of 105.6k chars. Code reported at github (not opened). Biggest threat to novelty of any family-#0 variant that is llama.cpp + SSD.

title: SpecExec: Massively Parallel Speculative Decoding for Interactive LLM Inference on Consumer Devices (Svirschevski, May, Chen et al.; arXiv 2406.02532v3, 30 Nov 2024)
setting: Llama-2-70B (target) + Llama-2-7B draft; A100 with emulated RAM offload, batch 1; consumer GPUs 4090/4060/3090/2080Ti over PCIe; baselines SpecInfer and sequential offloaded decoding
headline: Table 1 A100: 3.12 tok/s (18.7x) vs SpecInfer 1.34 tok/s (8.0x); 4-bit target about 6.0 tok/s (8.9x); Table 3 consumer GPUs, 4-bit 70B: RTX 4090 5.66 tok/s (8.3x), 3090 3.68, 4060 3.28, 2080Ti 1.86
caveat: Dense model: verifying a huge tree costs the same weight read as one token, so the gain is large; for an MoE the union grows with the tree, which is exactly why the MoE papers above exist. Speedups are vs sequential offloaded decoding, on GPU+PCIe, with 140GB RAM for 16-bit.
notes: Shows the dense upper bound; not transferable as a number to MoE.

title: Utility-Driven Speculative Decoding for Mixture-of-Experts (Cascade; Saxena, Tsai, Taneja, Jaleel, Qureshi; arXiv 2506.20675v1, 17 Jun 2025)
setting: Mixtral-8x7B FP8, Phi-3.5 FP8, OLMoE FP8, DeepSeek-V1 FP16, Qwen-1.5 FP16; one RTX 6000 Ada 48GB, i9-14900K, 64GB; vLLM 0.6.6; single-batch; n-gram drafter (main), EAGLE on Mixtral only; static K 1-3 vs K=0
headline: Verification data movement 2-3x; static K slows decode up to 1.5x (worst losses 26/38/54% at K=1/2/3, Fig 13); Cascade caps slowdown about 5%, +7-14% over best static K, up to 1.6x over no speculation; OLMoE 29% vs static K=3 33%
caveat: No expert offloading or caching in the evaluation (offloading only in related work). Experts GPU-resident, so the cost is HBM, not disk. Useful direction: speculation can lose on MoE; Cascade is a throttle.
notes: Abstract says 2-3x data movement; catalog says 'up to 3x'. Note: pubtech/A.md labels Cascade P-0039; in TESTLIST P-0039 is the s1 #5 row, the s1 #1 Cascade row is P-0010.

title: MoE-Spec: expert budgeting for speculative decoding (same paper as P-0002; alphaxiv page)
setting: see P-0002; page is the alphaxiv summary of arXiv 2602.16052
headline: OLMoE 127-token draft tree activates 54 of 64 experts per layer; top 32 of 64 experts hold 93% of routing probability; 10-30% over EAGLE-3; Mixtral MBPP 2.3x vs 1.7x
caveat: Same as P-0002: GPU-resident, budget is lossy, single request.
notes: Duplicate paper of P-0002 and P-0011 (screen listed it in two families).

title: AcceptMoE: Commitment-Weighted Self-Sizing Verifier Expert Sets for Efficient MoE Speculative Decoding (Liang, Chen, Mo, Wang, Li, Ma, Luk; Imperial/Tile-AI; arXiv 2608.02989v1, 4 Aug 2026)
setting: Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, GPT-OSS-120B with EAGLE-3 drafts; SGLang batch 1; full-residency on RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell; offloading on RTX 5090 32GB with a 48-slot expert pool per layer, full weights in pinned host RAM (not SSD); baseline = standard SD with natural routing
headline: 1.290x with all experts on GPU (Fig 3); 2.06x under offloading (Fig 4, text only gives the mean); host-to-device traffic -73.6 to -77.1%; cache hit +10.8-14.2 pts; mean accuracy -0.27 points over 12 model-task pairs
caveat: Closest idea to a cache-aware verify: eligibility of experts in the verifier is conditioned on what is already resident. Gains come from a lossy restriction of the verifier routing and from a baseline that thrashes a 48-slot pool; PCIe to GPU from RAM, not SSD to CPU.
notes: If our #0/#1 variants restrict the union to resident experts, this is prior art. Per-pair values only in figures.

title: MoE-SpeQ / SP-MoE / DraftExpert / S2-MoE (speculation plus expert prefetch) - row links SP-MoE html v2
headline: MoE-SpeQ up to 2.34x (abstract) / 3.3x (Sec 4.2); SP-MoE 1.07-3.5x; DraftExpert 1.45x avg; S2-MoE about 2.0x avg
caveat: Catalog says all 'use GPU/PCIe offload': true for SP-MoE and MoE-SpeQ, not for DraftExpert-MN (phone Flash, llama.cpp) or S2-MoE (Jetson SSD, llama.cpp).
notes: Bundle row; each paper graded individually above.

title: Hiding offloading latency with speculative decoding (SpecMoEOff, same paper as P-0005; arXiv PDF link)
setting: see P-0005 (read via the html version of the same paper)
headline: SD adds 1.53x / 1.45x; up to 2.5x vs MoE-Lightning; global batch 515-824
caveat: The amortisation argument holds only with a very large batch; with one sequence the extra tokens bring more experts, not more reuse.
notes: PDF link not directly readable by the fetch tool; content taken from html v1 of the same arXiv id.

title: EStream: Fast and Memory-Efficient MoE Prefill through Expert Virtualization on Mobile NPUs (Zhang, Zheng, Wu, Huang, Wu; arXiv 2609.06551v1, Sep 2026)
setting: OLMoE-1B-7B (16 layers, 64 experts), LFM2.5-8B-A1B, DeepSeek-V2-Lite; also Qwen3-30B-A3B and Mixtral-8x7B (Table 3); OnePlus phone, 15.1 GiB, Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 NPU, UFS 4.1; Q4; baselines llama.cpp-CPU, MNN, ONNX Runtime, EdgeMoE, PowerInfer-style streaming
headline: Pure-prefill TTFT 2.25-27.57x faster than the fastest baseline (abstract, Fig 8); peak memory 6.45-12.29x lower; 4K tokens: 2.12 s OLMoE vs 58.45 s fastest non-offloading competitor; Fig 3(a): 80.1-98.1% of layer-expert pairs activated at 512 tokens, 92.4-100% at 4K
caveat: Directly supports a high prefill union (our 0.75-0.95 assumption; our decode-trace proxy reached only 0.55-0.61). But models have 32-64 experts, top-6/8, where union saturates faster than 512 experts top-10; phone NPU, not CPU; prefill only; CPU runtimes win below 66-80 tokens.
notes: Page read to 100k of 111k chars. Quote: demand-paged mmap delays rather than eliminates residency.

title: Fate: Fast Edge Inference of MoE Models via Cross-Layer Gate (Fang, Hong, Huang et al.; arXiv 2502.12224v2, 7 May 2025)
setting: DeepSeekMoE-16B (6 of 64) and Qwen1.5-MoE-14.3B (4 of 60); RTX 3090 24GB + i9-9900X 128GB PCIe3; RTX 1080Ti + 64GB PCIe1; baselines load-on-demand and an activation-path method
headline: Prefill (Fig 11) up to 4.5x over LoD, 1.9x over EAP (high-end PC); 804 tok/s DeepSeekMoE at 512-token prompt; decode up to 4.1x / 2.2x; on MMLU Qwen1.5-MoE activates on average 55.9 of 60 experts per layer in prefill; prefetch accuracy 78.79% (97.15% with extra)
caveat: Confirms prefill touches almost all experts (55.9/60). But catalog 'no sorting scheme' is not quite right: Fate orders prefill transfers by expert popularity and sends the least popular as INT2 (lossy). GPU+PCIe, small models.

title: DAOP: Data-Aware Offloading and Predictive Pre-Calculation for Efficient MoE Inference (Zhang, Aggarwal, Mitra; arXiv 2501.10375v3)
setting: Mixtral-8x7B and Phi-3.5-MoE; RTX A6000 48GB + i9-10980XE 130GB, PCIe4; batch 1; baselines MoE-OnDemand, DeepSpeed-MII, Mixtral-Offloading, Fiddler
headline: Abstract up to 8.20x vs caching/prefetching and 1.35x vs offloading; Fig 9 +40.4% over Fiddler (4.52 tok/s Mixtral, 8.21 Phi-3.5, 46.9% cache ratio); Fig 10 avg +35.4%; Table IV energy 14.37 vs 10.06 tok/kJ
caveat: Per-expert token counts in prefill drive which experts live on the GPU; CPU computes the rest. Top-2 models, GPU decides, 130 GB host RAM. Accuracy falls on GSM8K with a small cache. The 8.20x comparison is not itemised in the text.
notes: Read through the arXiv html version (the PDF link returned binary).

title: Fiddler: CPU-GPU Orchestration for Fast Inference of Mixture-of-Experts Models (Kamahori, Tang, Gu, Zhu, Kasikci; arXiv 2402.07033v3; venue not on the page, ICLR 2025 from memory)
setting: Mixtral-8x7B 16-bit (>90 GB); Quadro RTX 6000 24GB + Xeon 6126; RTX 6000 Ada 48GB + Xeon 8480+; host RAM not stated; baselines DeepSpeed-MII, Mixtral-Offloading, llama.cpp b2956; single request
headline: Single-request decode 1.26x avg (Fig 4); long prefill 1.30x avg (Fig 5; Sec 4.2: 1.07x vs DeepSpeed-MII, 1.65x vs Mixtral-Offloading TTFT); beam search 11.57x vs llama.cpp (Fig 6)
caveat: Numbers match. CPU expert compute is only attractive when a GPU exists and the PCIe copy is slower than CPU compute; the whole model sits in host RAM (>90 GB), no SSD. Our regime is already CPU-only.
notes: Mechanism for prefill (compute on CPU vs copy) was taken from the catalog; I read the numbers, not a prefill-specific mechanism statement. Page read via html version.

title: FlashMoE: Reducing SSD I/O Bottlenecks via ML-Based Cache Replacement for MoE Inference on Edge Devices (Kim, Lee, Han, Yoo, Kim; arXiv 2601.17063v2, Jan 2026)
setting: OLMoE-1B-7B and Qwen3-30B-A3B; Ryzen 5 9600X, RTX 5070 Ti 16GB, PCIe5 NVMe 7.4 GB/s, 4x16GB DDR5 (about 1GB left free, rest locked), batch for eval not stated; baselines Fiddler, DAOP, llama.cpp, HF; policies LRU/LFU/ARC/LeCaR
headline: 4x faster initial load than llama.cpp, 6.8x than Fiddler/DAOP (Sec 4.2); prefill 2.5x over llama.cpp, 4.1x over Fiddler/DAOP (Fig 7); hit rate up to +21% vs LRU (OLMoE, Fig 6); decode +22% vs LRU on OLMoE but about +7% on Qwen3-30B; abstract 'up to 2.6x'; prefill touches about 47% of experts at 32 tokens and about 67% at longer
caveat: Real SSD+DRAM numbers, nearest on storage, but GPU 16GB, 64GB DRAM, 7.4 GB/s, tiny models; '4x load' is start-up of non-expert weights, not throughput; ML policy trained on TriviaQA traces with a Belady oracle; gain over LRU shrinks on the larger model (7%).
notes: Read via html version. 2.6x in the abstract is not traced in the body.

title: llama : add Mixtral support (llama.cpp PR #4406; slaren, ggerganov; opened 11 Dec 2023, merged 13 Dec 2023)
setting: Q4_0 Mixtral-8x7B on M2 Ultra (one timing log): 9.00 ms/token prompt (about 111 tok/s), 18.67 ms/token generation (about 53.6 tok/s)
headline: Introduces ggml_mul_mat_id; author states it is efficient for BS=1 but not so much for BS>1 because batched tokens are evaluated separately, improvements planned
caveat: Catalog says the op already processes batched tokens per expert; at merge the PR says the opposite for BS>1. Later versions may have grouped tokens (from memory, not checked). Our own plan to remove the ids->ne[1]!=1 filter shows the current code differs from this PR.
notes: Page read to 100k of 171k chars; no mul_mat_id-specific benchmark.

title: Flash-MoE: Running a 397B-parameter model on a 48GB MacBook (Ikesan / lilting channel, 23 Mar 2026; secondary article about a public project)
setting: Qwen3.5-397B-A17B (60 layers, 512 experts, 4 activated per token in the build described; model default is 10 per a web search, not on the page); M3 Max 48GB, 1TB SSD; 4-bit 209GB; batch 1; no custom cache (OS page cache about 71% hit)
headline: 4.36 tok/s (4-bit, FMA-optimised), 3.90 baseline, 5.74 tok/s 2-bit (breaks JSON/tool calls); SSD 17.5 GB/s; I/O 2.41 ms of 4.28 ms per layer; one token reads about 27 MB per layer set (6.75 MB per expert); prefetching -73%, mmap x0.2, LZ4 -13%
caveat: 512 experts per layer, SSD streaming, 48GB: the nearest in model shape to ours. But a 17.4 GB/s Apple SSD, no prefill benchmark, no quality evaluation of the 10->4 expert cut (the article gives 397B in title and 497B in body). Blog, not peer reviewed, numbers from author.
notes: Relevant to family #3 as well: the project reduces the active experts per token to 4 to fit the SSD budget; independent write-ups dispute the quality cost (search results, not verified).

title: Not All Experts are Equal: Efficient Expert Pruning and Skipping for MoE LLMs (NAEE; Lu, Liu, Xu, Zhou, Huang, Zhang, Yan, Li; arXiv 2402.14800, 22 Feb 2024, v2 30 May 2024; ACL 2024 per page comments)
setting: Mixtral-8x7B and Instruct only (top-2 of 8); 2x A100-80G originally; AutoGPTQ-based generation script; batch not reported
headline: Pruning r=6: 1.20x, r=4: 1.27x; plus dynamic skipping: 1.23x (r=6), 1.31x (r=4), Instruct 1.27x/1.33x; avg 8-task accuracy 67.58 -> 64.22 (r=6) -> 59.57 (r=4) (text says -2.9/-7.1, table implies -3.4/-8.0)
caveat: Top-2 of 8, so 'skip the second expert' is the only skip; speedups from a single script; quality drops sharply on GSM8K without domain-matched calibration. Gives no evidence for 10 -> 6 on a 512-expert model.
notes: Read via html version (PDF link binary; abstract has no numbers).

title: Opportunistic Expert Activation: Batch-Aware Expert Routing for Faster Decode Without Retraining (Oncescu, Wu, Chung et al., Together AI / Dao; arXiv 2511.02237, 4 Nov 2025)
setting: Qwen3-30B-A3B (one H100 80GB) and Qwen3-235B-A22B (8xH100 TP), bf16, SGLang; batch up to 16; baseline vanilla top-8
headline: MoE-layer latency -39% (30B, k0=3: 106.8 vs 175.7 us) and -15% (235B, k0=5); accuracy at k0=3 (30B): AIME 80.0 vs 80.4, GPQA 58.6 vs 60.2, LiveCodeBench 61.2 vs 62.1, MATH-500 93.5 vs 92.8 (Table 6); the 43.0->22.2 (AIME24) and 51.6->26.5 (GPQA) figures are average ACTIVATED EXPERTS per layer (Table 4), not accuracy
caveat: Catalog reads expert-count numbers as an accuracy collapse. In fact quality barely moves, because OEA fills each token's extra experts from the set already loaded for other tokens in the batch. That mechanism has nothing to fill from at batch 1. Latency is per MoE layer, not end-to-end.
notes: ERROR ALSO IN pubtech/A.md line 105 ('large drops ... when k is lowered to 3'). Correct reading: the paper is evidence for batch-aware reuse, not for or against a plain top-k cut. Read via html version.

title: LExI: Layer-Adaptive Active Experts for Efficient MoE Model Inference (Chitty-Venkata, Madireddy, Emani, Vishwanath; Argonne; arXiv 2509.02753v1, 2 Sep 2025)
setting: Mixtral-8x7B, Qwen1.5-MoE, OLMoE-1B-7B, MiniCPM-MoE, DeepSeek-V2-Lite, DeepSeek-VL2-Tiny; H100 80GB (2-4 GPUs), vLLM, batch 16; baselines NAEE and MoE-I2 pruning (12.5/25/50%)
headline: Same throughput as pruning with about 10% better accuracy (abstract); Qwen1.5-MoE >=+5.1% throughput vs pruning (Fig 4); OLMoE B=100 matches 50% intra-pruning throughput at about +10% accuracy; DeepSeek-V2-Lite +6.5% throughput at equal accuracy
caveat: Compares against pruning, not against the unmodified model; results in figures only; '+10%' may be absolute points or relative; no memory reduction; GPU batch 16 throughput. Per-layer top-k allocation is a real idea for us (sensitive early layers) but no number applies.

title: REAP the Experts: Why Pruning Prevails for One-Shot MoE Compression (Lasby, Lazarevich, Sinnadurai, Lie, Ioannou, Thangarasa; Cerebras; arXiv 2510.13999, v1 15 Oct 2025, v3 13 May 2026; ICLR 2026 not on the page)
setting: Seven SMoE models, ERNIE-4.5-21B to Kimi-K2 (about 1T); hardware not given in the part read; baselines frequency/EAN pruning, M-SMoE, HC-SMoE merging; no latency measured
headline: Table 3 at 50%: Qwen3-Coder-480B code avg 0.660 -> 0.644, MC 0.750 -> 0.692; Kimi-K2 code 0.659 -> 0.646, MC 0.780 -> 0.643, tool-use 0.666 -> 0.564
caveat: Near-lossless only on code with domain-matched calibration (C4 calibration collapsed code); multiple-choice and tool-use drop clearly. It removes half the experts, i.e. halves the file (a different lever from top-k cut: smaller footprint, not fewer reads per token). No speed measured.
notes: Calibrate-on-domain requirement is a hard constraint for a general laptop assistant. Page read to 100k of 144k chars.

title: SliceMoE: Bit-Sliced Expert Caching under Miss-Rate Constraints for Efficient MoE Inference (Choi, Kim, Oh et al., KAIST; arXiv 2512.12990v3, 12 Mar 2026)
setting: DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B; MODELED hardware: XPU 16.4 TOPS, 8GB LPDDR4, UFS 3.1 flash 10 Gbps, expert cache 1.8/2.4/3.6 GB; batch 1; GSM8K only; baselines Cache-Prior and Cumsum routing
headline: Decode energy up to 2.37x / 2.85x lower and speed up to 1.81x / 1.64x (Fig 9); cache warm-up in prefill: 2.31x energy, 1.96x speed vs empty cache (Fig 10)
caveat: Closest regime on the storage side (flash to small DRAM cache, batch 1), and caching more low-bit slices instead of fewer full ones is the claim we test in the 2/3/4-bit family. But results are from an architectural model, accuracy only on GSM8K, plain LRU, 16B-class models.

title: DyMoE: Dynamic Expert Orchestration with Mixed-Precision Quantization for Efficient MoE Inference on Edge (Huang, Fang, Luo, Chen, Zheng, Wu; arXiv 2603.19172v1, 19 Mar 2026)
setting: Mixtral-8x7B and Qwen3-30B-A3B; EPYC 7542 + RTX 3090 with VRAM capped to 12-24GB; experts in host RAM over PCIe3 (SSD not evaluated); batch 1; baselines Accelerate, Mixtral-Offloading, MoE-Infinity, Fiddler
headline: TTFT 3.44-22.7x lower (22.7x vs Fiddler, 24GB); TPOT up to 14.58x vs Fiddler (Mixtral, 16GB), 8.31x vs Accelerate, 2.27x vs Mixtral-Offloading; Table 3 ablation TPOT 0.2795 -> 0.0656 s at 24GB; Mixtral MMLU 0.6807 vs Int4 0.6795
caveat: Big ratios are against weak baselines (Fiddler, Accelerate); against the strongest baseline 2.27x. The title says SSD/edge; the evaluation is GPU + host RAM; the 'zero calibration' claim sits oddly with GPTQ; the 14.58x is used for both TTFT and TPOT in different places.

title: MoE top_k override (--moe-top-k) guide, vllm-mlx (author not stated)
setting: Qwen3-30B-A3B-4bit on Apple M4 Max 128GB, batch 1, greedy; whole model resident in RAM
headline: Decode 126.5 tok/s (k=8) -> 136.1 (k=6) -> 140.3 (k=5) -> 147.3 tok/s (k=4), +16.5%; quality table all TBD; first 16 tokens identical on probe prompts; 3-bit + top_k=4 broke output in a smoke test
caveat: Compute-bound residency, so it measures only the Amdahl part (our 1.19x ceiling is consistent). No quality data; 30B-A3B with 128 experts, not a 512-expert model. Recommends top_k=4 floor and one aggressive knob at a time.

title: DraftExpert: Expansion-Aware Self-Speculative Decoding for End-Device MoE Inference (Dengke Han, arXiv 2607.24434 v1, 27 Jul 2026, preprint, 9 pp)
url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.24434 (abstract read via /abs and full text via /html)
setting: DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Moonlight-16B-A3B (27 layers, 64 routed + 2 shared, top-6). Two platforms: RTX 4090 24 GB with experts in host RAM (BF16, PCIe), and Snapdragon 8 Elite phone (Hexagon NPU, llama.cpp Q4_0, experts staged from flash). Baseline: autoregressive expert-offloaded decoding on the same platform, plus best training-free shared+top-r drafter.
headline: Table 2: speedup vs AR 1.36x (DS, GPU, 2.19->2.99 tok/s), 1.52x (DS, phone, 10.18->15.47), 1.29x (ML, GPU, 1.94->2.50), 1.61x (ML, phone, 8.50->13.69); average 1.45x; acceptance 84-87%, prefetch hit 86-88% (abstract). Training-free top-r drafter is slower than AR in all four cells.
transfers_to_us: No. Needs a trained per-layer draft expert (training cost not reported), models are 16B with 64 experts, GPU or NPU compute, and the AR baseline has no stated LRU size. The phone flash path (10 tok/s for a 16B Q4_0 model) is nowhere near disk-bound like a 69 GB file on 8-32 GB RAM.
caveat: Only 2 small models and 2 setups; baseline cache policy unspecified; about 12-14% of prefetched experts are wasted; gain is against AR, not against AR plus a tuned cache.
notes: The page itself says exact verification still exposes expert misses, i.e. the union cost is real; consistent with our byte finding but the paper avoids it by a fixed-footprint draft path (shared + top-1 + trained draft expert), which is a different idea from 'k positions expert-major'.

title: AcceptMoE: Commitment-Weighted Self-Sizing Verifier Expert Sets for Efficient MoE Speculative Decoding (Liang, Chen, Mo, Wang, Li, Ma, Luk; Imperial College London / Tile-AI; arXiv 2608.02989 v1, 4 Aug 2026)
setting: Qwen3-Instruct, Qwen3-Coder (30B-A3B class) and GPT-OSS-120B; EAGLE-3 draft tree (64 draft tokens), SGLang, batch 1, greedy, 256 tokens, 20 prompts, median of 3. Resident: RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell. Offload: RTX 5090 32 GB, 48 expert slots per layer on GPU, experts in pinned host RAM (BF16; GPT-OSS native MXFP4). Baselines: Vanilla AR, Standard SD (EAGLE-3 with native routing), MoE-Spec-style fixed budgets.
headline: Mean 1.290x over Standard SD with all experts resident (range 1.217-1.339x over 12 model-task pairs); 2.06x over Standard SD under physical offloading; H2D traffic per output token -73.6% to -77.1% and cache hit +10.8 to +14.2 points vs Standard SD (Table 2); mean accuracy 0.27 points below Standard SD; residency-aware pruning alone cuts traffic 38.6-48.6% and adds 4.6-15.1% throughput.
transfers_to_us: Partly, as evidence for the direction only. It confirms that Standard SD moves MORE expert bytes than vanilla AR under offloading and has a lower hit rate, which matches our simulation (k>1 does not beat an LRU path). But AcceptMoE's win comes from restricting which experts the target may use (a lossy change to the model's routing), on PCIe host RAM, with a 32 GB GPU holding 48 slots/layer.
caveat: 2.06x is relative to Standard SD, not to AR with a good cache; the method changes the output distribution (accuracy -0.27 pts mean, per-pair -1.83 to +1.22); GPU-resident dense parts, draft model and KV on GPU.
notes: Text says Standard SD is faster than Vanilla AR on all four GPT-OSS pairs under offload, so SD can still beat AR there; the paper gives no k=1-with-large-LRU baseline in our sense. A 125B model (GPT-OSS-120B) is among the targets but with GPU-resident slots.

title: MoE-Spec: Expert Budgeting for Efficient Speculative Decoding (McDanel, Li, Surineni, Khaitan; arXiv 2602.16052 v1, 17 Feb 2026, cs.LG)
setting: OLMoE-1B-7B (64 experts, k=8), Qwen3-30B-A3B (128, k=8), Mixtral-8x7B (8, k=2); EAGLE-3 (EAGLE-1 for Mixtral), tree of 63 tokens; NVIDIA A100 80 GB (Mixtral on 2 GPUs); 80 samples per benchmark, 5 benchmarks; experts fully resident in HBM (no offloading experiments).
headline: Speedup over EAGLE in 27 of 30 model-benchmark configs; average relative gain 27% (Mixtral), 16% (Qwen3-30B), 6% (OLMoE); example Mixtral MBPP T=0 2.3x vs EAGLE 1.7x; OLMoE: a 127-token tree activates 54 of 64 experts per layer (Fig. 2b); at tree 255 EAGLE-3 loads 54 experts for 1.85x, MoE-Spec loads 32 for 2.1x (Fig. 4). Abstract: 10-30% over EAGLE-3.
transfers_to_us: No for the speedup (HBM-bound A100, nothing offloaded, comparison is to EAGLE-3). Yes for the premise: the union of experts of a draft tree approaches the whole layer at tree sizes 30-100, which is the same mechanism as our union-fraction measure.
caveat: Lossy: experts outside the budget are substituted, quality kept 'within one standard deviation' of EAGLE; the authors note EAGLE uses q(x)=1 so T=1 output is not exactly lossless even for the baseline.
notes: Paper says it 'applies on top of compressed or offloaded models' but does not test offloading.

title: Reddit post snapshot (sentinel-team mirror, 2026-07-17), u/Sleepybear2611: running a 754B MoE on a consumer desktop; low reliability
setting: GLM-5.2 754B (365 GB IQ4_XS) on RTX 5080 16 GB + RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB, Ryzen 9700X, 31 GB RAM, WD SN7100 NVMe (5.7 GB/s sustained). Self-reported, repo linked, 3 comments captured.
headline: 0.9 tok/s final (from 0.2) via prefetching, top-4 instead of top-8, pinned hot experts, direct-read streamer; about 3.4 GB of experts touched per token vs 5.7 GB/s drive gives a 1.55 tok/s ceiling; CPU expert compute caps at about 2.8 tok/s; a 0.70x smaller quant gave the same 0.9 tok/s (bytes streamed per token unchanged); top 1.7% of expert slots take 25% of routings. Claims MTP/Medusa/lookahead do not pay off and that predicting the working set from the prompt loses to a reactive LRU.
transfers_to_us: Qualitatively yes (NVMe-bound, batch 1, tiny RAM relative to model, LRU beats prediction), but it is one anecdotal run with two GPUs; the 'greedy decoding already reads only needed experts' reading in the catalog is not stated as such on the page, the claim is that spec decoding does not pay off.
caveat: Not peer reviewed, one commenter flagged it as AI-written, another asked to explain the RAM figures (63 GB 'fast memory' combines VRAM and RAM); details of the spec-decoding tests are in the linked repo, which I did not open.
notes: Useful sanity numbers: bytes-per-token governs speed (smaller file did not help), CPU compute ceiling 2.8 tok/s. 'a commenter disputed its RAM figures' is a mild paraphrase of a request for clarification.

title: MoE-Spec: Expert Budgeting for Efficient Speculative Decoding (same paper as P-0034)
setting: See P-0034 (A100 80 GB, OLMoE/Qwen3-30B/Mixtral, EAGLE-3, resident experts).
headline: 10-30% over EAGLE-3 (abstract); per-model average 6% / 16% / 27% (text); acceptance length down only 1.4% on average.
transfers_to_us: No for speedup (see P-0034). It is a verification-time budget, not a small resident draft plus confidence gate.
caveat: Lossy substitution; baseline EAGLE-3, not AR with cache.
notes: Duplicate of P-0034 in two families.

title: SP-MoE: Speculative Decoding and Prefetching for Accelerating MoE-based Model Inference (Chen, Wen, Wu, Zhang, Wu; Sun Yat-sen Univ / HKU; arXiv 2510.10302 v2, 6 Nov 2025, cs.DC, 14 pp)
setting: Mixtral 8x7B (draft: a Mixtral-offloading-style small model), Phi-3.5-MoE (draft Phi-mini-MoE), DeepSeek-V2-Lite (draft AWQ). Three servers: RTX 3090 / RTX 4090 / A100 40 GB with 512 GB-1 TB host RAM over PCIe 4.0 x16; batch 1; TPOT metric. Baselines: Mixtral-Offloading+SD, AdapMoE, MoE-Infinity, SpecMoE-style.
headline: TPOT speedup 1.07x-3.5x over baselines (abstract); 1.35x average over baselines across 4 datasets, peak 1.75x vs Mixtral-Offloading on HumanEval (3090), min 1.12x vs AdapMoE (4090) (Fig. 9); 2.3x average across 3 models, peak 3.5x with DeepSeek-V2-Lite on A100 (Fig. 10); TPOT -6.9% to -71.4% vs three baselines.
transfers_to_us: No. All experts sit in host DRAM behind PCIe 4.0 and a GPU does the compute; per-expert sizes are 336 MB (Mixtral) to 16 MB (DeepSeek). It shows that the draft model's gating network predicts target experts (top-1 prediction accuracy 88.9% DeepSeek, 56-60% Mixtral/Phi), which is a prefetch idea, not an expert-major union idea.
caveat: Baselines are other GPU-offloading systems, not a tuned LRU path; speedup depends strongly on GPU (largest on 3090).
notes: Catalog's first clause (rejected draft tokens waste I/O bandwidth) is plausible from the abstract (SD 'aggravates bandwidth contention') but I did not locate that exact claim; the preloading-during-drafting part is correct.

title: Utility-Driven Speculative Decoding for Mixture-of-Experts, 'Cascade' (Saxena, Taneja, Qureshi, Tsai, Jaleel; Georgia Tech / NVIDIA; arXiv 2506.20675 v1, 17 Jun 2025; MICRO 2025 per page header)
setting: Mixtral 8x7B (FP8), Phi-3.5-MoE (FP8), OLMoE (FP8), DeepSeek-V1 and Qwen-1.5-MoE (FP16), vLLM, single-batch, RTX 6000 Ada 48 GB + i9-14900K 64 GB; n-gram speculation (EAGLE only on Mixtral). Models fit on the GPU, no offloading.
headline: Speculation can slow MoE decoding: static K=1/2/3 slowdowns up to 26%/38%/54%; draft tokens raise verification data movement 2-3x; Cascade caps worst case at about 5% and beats best static K by 7-14% on average; Mixtral code +57% vs +39% for static K=3; OLMoE Cascade 29% vs 31%/33% static; utility predicts speedup with R^2 99.4% over 120 points.
transfers_to_us: Direction yes (speculation can lose because of expert union cost; decide by utility), numbers no (in-GPU, FP8, n-gram drafts, not disk).
caveat: Not an offloading paper; on OLMoE it is slightly worse than best static K; the 'when to speculate' logic would need re-profiling in a disk-bound regime.
notes: Strong support for treating K as adaptive and for the claim that naive SD can be 1.5x slower for MoE.

title: Faster Cascades via Speculative Decoding (Narasimhan, Jitkrittum, Rawat, Kim, Gupta, Menon, Kumar; Google Research; arXiv 2405.19261 v2, 21 Oct 2024)
setting: Dense models only: T5-small drafter with T5-large / T5-XL verifier (WMT, XSum, CNN/DM), Gemma v2 2B->27B (and 2B->9B) few-shot on 8 benchmarks. Batch 1 wall-clock latency; hardware not stated in the text I read (first 100k of 160k characters).
headline: Table 2 (T5, T=1, gamma=5): SpecCascade[Token] latency vs large model 1.85x / 1.18x / 1.89x (small->large) and 2.50x / 1.40x / 1.89x (small->XL) on WMT / XSum / CNN-DM; lossy SpecDecode small->XL 2.17x / 1.28x / 2.07x; same-latency quality 22.50 BLEU (WMT) for small->large.
transfers_to_us: Gate half only, and conceptually. It is a quality/cost trade (deferral rules), not lossless; no MoE, no offloading. Venue 'ICLR 2025' in the catalog is not shown on the page I read (from memory it was ICLR 2025: unverified here).
caveat: Output is not distribution-preserving; relies on calibration of both models; sequential cascades do better at low latency.
notes: Supports the gate/deferral concept as known art; says nothing about expert I/O.

title: hackmd note by thc1006: single-user llama.cpp MoE speculative decoding test (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B), versions v1-v5 (April-May 2026)
setting: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B quantized, one RTX 3090 (model fully on GPU, baseline about 136 tok/s), llama.cpp: n-gram cache, ngram-mod, small draft model, DFlash; later 2x3090 with vLLM MTP.
headline: v1: no mode beat baseline, decode -3 to -12% even at 100% acceptance; v2: best draft-model setting about 39% slower; v3: DFlash about 45% slower at best, but vLLM MTP +27.5% on 2x3090 (claim of general regression retracted); v5: errata, some accuracy results need retest.
transfers_to_us: No. GPU-resident model, 3B active, not disk-bound. The catalog's 'about 54% slower' is not on the page (I find 39% and 45%), and the page later reports a speedup with MTP on vLLM, so 'no speculative mode beat baseline' is only the v1 llama.cpp result.
caveat: One tester, not peer reviewed, repeatedly revised; author links earlier losses partly to prefix-cache interaction and flag mismatch.
notes: Evidence that llama.cpp-side spec decoding for small-active MoE can be net negative when compute-bound; no I/O information.

title: ReMoE: Boosting Expert Reuse through Router Fine-Tuning in Memory-Constrained MoE LLM Inference (Zhu, Liao, Jiang, Zhang, Wang, Xiao; Beihang; arXiv 2605.27081 v1, 26 May 2026; ICML 2026 poster per search listing)
setting: DeepSeek-V2-Lite (15.7B, 64 experts) and Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B; gate-only router fine-tune, 2,000 steps, about 7.9 h on one 80 GB GPU (appendix). Real systems: vLLM GPU-CPU expert offload on RTX 3090 (cache 6 experts/layer, concurrency 1) and llama.cpp on Jetson Orin NX 16 GB with the model on a PCIe Gen3 x4 NVMe, --mmap, -np 1, -n 128.
headline: Expert overlap +26.4% (DeepSeek-V2-Lite), +27.2% (Qwen1.5-MoE). Table 3 (LRU, C=6): uHR 0.3187 -> 0.3687 (+15.7% relative), unique misses 0.8707M -> 0.8068M. Table 4 (vLLM 3090): 3.58 -> 3.88 tok/s (+8.4%), TPOT -4.5%. Table 5 (Jetson/llama.cpp): TPOT 554.69 -> 306.27 ms (ShareGPT, -44.8%), 613.73 -> 346.04 (GSM8K, -43.6%), 672.68 -> 337.61 (HumanEval, -49.8%), decode 1.77-1.99x. Table 6: MMLU +0.09, HumanEval +2.44, GSM8K -0.76 pp.
transfers_to_us: Partly, and it is the closest evidence in our regime (SSD-backed, llama.cpp, batch 1, tiny cache of 6 experts per layer). But: model is 15.7B, not 125B; the gate-only fine-tune of a 125B model needs far more than one GPU; the Jetson baseline decodes at under 2 tok/s via mmap, so a 15.7% hit-rate gain turning into 44-50% lower TPOT suggests the mmap/page-cache path amplifies misses (my inference); the vLLM PCIe result is only +8.4%.
caveat: Requires fine-tuning (calibration data OpenHermes-2.5 per the text); the paper's own conservative number is the +8.4% vLLM one; quality tested on small benchmarks only.
notes: Our simulated f=0.5 stickiness (hit 0.763 vs 0.549 at 2 footprints, 1.33x serial) is a much larger perturbation than ReMoE's +5 points absolute uHR at C=6; the paper also has a CE-only control showing generic router fine-tuning makes things worse (EOR 0.2293 vs 0.2730).

title: Mixture of Cache-Conditional Experts for Efficient Mobile Device Inference (Skliar, van Rozendaal, Lepert, Boinovski, van Baalen, Nagel, Whatmough, Ehteshami Bejnordi; Qualcomm AI Research; arXiv 2412.00099, v1 27 Nov 2024, v3 24 Jun 2025; TMLR 06/2025)
setting: Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B on llama.cpp CPU, two Snapdragon Android 14 phones: 12 GB (4-bit, cache 30 of 60 experts) and 16 GB (8-bit, cache 45); other models (DeepSeek-V2, Phi-3.5-MoE, Mixtral-8x7B) simulation only. Training-free cache-prior reranking. Reference 1x is the best LRU throughput over cache sizes.
headline: 'Over 2x' speedup over best LRU on-device (text; relative throughput only, no absolute tok/s). Miss rate LRU -> cache-prior at lambda=0.5: Qwen1.5 35% -> 16%, DeepSeek-V2 28% -> 7%, Phi-3.5 22% -> 9%, Mixtral 40% -> 21%. Wikitext perplexity +0.1% to +3%; MMLU and GSM8K drops under 0.1% (abstract).
transfers_to_us: Partly. CPU-only llama.cpp batch 1 with a RAM cache and storage behind it matches our setting well; but the models are 14B-class and the cache is 50-75% of the experts, not 2-8 footprints of a 512-expert model; it is runtime (lossy) rerouting, not fine-tuning.
caveat: Tested only on Qwen1.5-MoE on phones; high lambda hurts; granular MoEs tolerate swaps better than Mixtral (miss rate 40% -> 21% only); results depend on mlock and OS memory behaviour.
notes: This is the inference-time twin of #6 and was published a year and a half before ReMoE; it makes the #6 idea (cache-biased routing) clearly known.

title: Not All Models Suit Expert Offloading: On Local Routing Consistency of Mixture-of-Expert Models (Liang, Wang, Tian, Li, Tang, Wei; Fudan / USC / Huawei; arXiv 2505.16056 v3, 10 Dec 2025; the catalog says ICLR 2026, not shown on the page)
setting: 20 MoE LLMs (3B-57B; Mixtral-8x7B, DeepSeek-V2-Lite, Qwen3, OLMoE, GRIN-MoE, Phi-3.5-MoE, ...) plus pretrained 1.43B 'TOY' models; 22,528 samples of 512 tokens; metrics SRP (best segment routing F1) and SCH (oracle segment cache hit rate). Hardware not given in the part I read (100k of 136k chars).
headline: At segment length 16 SRP ranges 19 (SwitchTransformers encoder) to 78 (LLaMA-MoE-v2), Mixtral about 49; cache of about 2x the active expert count (rho=2) balances hit rate and efficiency; TOY baseline at rho=2: SCH 90.55 vs LRU 67.04 vs LFU 70.87 (normalised to optimal).
transfers_to_us: Supports the operating point only loosely: 'about 2x active experts' is a per-layer cache (rho times top-k), which is the same as about 2 footprints, but the conclusion is derived from an oracle cache hit rate on 512-token texts, not from measured throughput; several models with shared experts show low consistency.
caveat: SCH assumes an oracle cache; size inconsistency 54B vs 57B on the page; appendix throughput discussion not read.
notes: Also says local load balance trades off against local routing consistency, a hint that stickiness has a quality cost at training time.

title: vLLM issue #38256, '[RFC]: Incremental MoE Expert Offloading - GPU Cache + Async Pipeline' (author e1n00r, opened 26 Mar 2026, still open, thread to 29 Sep 2026)
setting: GPU expert cache (LFRU) over CPU pinned memory; author's own tinyserve: 30 tok/s on an 8 GB RTX PRO 2000 with GPT-OSS-20B MXFP4, 97-100% hit rate. Comments from Apple Silicon, GB10, GB300, RTX PRO 6000, 2xA100 users.
headline: Batched prefill: one load per unique expert instead of per token, cited as 375x fewer loads at 3K context; Apple Silicon commenter: LFU pinning 1.4-2.3x worse than LRU, staging predicted experts 0.94-0.95x (slower), next-layer router reuse predicts experts 83.6-99.1%; GB10 comment: NVMe about 6.9 GB/s, expert-split prefill 7.2 s -> 0.29 s at 25% capacity but not bit-exact.
transfers_to_us: Mostly irrelevant to decode (the proposal is a GPU cache RFC; prefill dedup is the only overlap with our prefill idea). The catalog's '12K loads to 32 unique' and 'Edge0 switches to whole-layer' did not appear in the page text I read (it gives 375x). The Apple Silicon comment that prediction/staging is slower than plain LRU is relevant anecdotal support.
caveat: An issue thread: unreviewed numbers from many users, mixed hardware, no controlled benchmark.
notes: Not a method with a result table; treat as discussion, not evidence.

title: ExpertFlow: Optimized Expert Activation and Token Allocation / Predictive Expert Caching and Token Scheduling (He, Zhang, Tang, Shi, Wang, Zeng, Tang, Chu, Yin, Tsang, Ong; arXiv 2410.17954 v2 stamped 2 Apr 2026; DAC '26)
setting: Qwen1.5-MoE, DeepSeek-MoE, Mixtral-8x7B, Switch Transformers (32/64/128 experts); one NVIDIA A40 48 GB + Xeon Gold 6338; baselines Cache-MoE (per-layer LRU), SE-MoE and Pregated-MoE (Switch only).
headline: Cache hit ratio 91.96% vs LRU up to 61.15% lower (ablation only on Switch-32, where the stated gain is 15-36%); throughput vs Cache-MoE up to 1.99x (Mixtral), 2.12x (Qwen1.5), 1.94x (DeepSeek-MoE); up to 10x vs SE-MoE on Switch-128; GPU memory -93.72% vs all-in-GPU; predictor accuracy up to 95%.
transfers_to_us: No. It is a learned routing-path predictor plus token scheduler on a GPU, batched token groups, not a router-stickiness method; the '61% better than LRU' comes from the Switch-32 ablation. 'Without changing the router' is correct.
caveat: Memory savings are against all-in-GPU; predictor compared only to simple heuristics; token scheduler helps only on Switch models.
notes: Strengthens the point that predictive caching beats LRU on GPU, but there is no evidence for a 2-footprint CPU cache.

title: Fast Inference of Mixture-of-Experts Language Models with Offloading (Eliseev, Mazur; MIPT / Yandex; arXiv 2312.17238 v1, 28 Dec 2023)
setting: Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct, HQQ mixed quantization (4-bit attention + 2- or 3-bit experts, about 2.6 bits/param for 2-bit experts with metadata); T4 (Colab, PCIe3), RTX 3060 12 GB, RTX 3080 Mobile 16 GB, A100; per-layer LRU cache of k experts (k=2 on 3060, 4 elsewhere) plus speculative expert pre-loading; batch 1.
headline: Table 2 (2-bit experts, full algorithm): 3.061 / 2.655 / 2.278 / 2.092 tok/s on A100 / 3080 Mobile / 3060 / T4; without pre-loading 2.918 / 2.227 / 2.051 / 1.567; without LRU and pre-loading 2.265 / 1.758 / 1.547 / 1.168; naive offloading 1.392 / 1.059 / 0.919 / 0.661. Table 1: Mixtral MMLU 70.51% FP16 vs 66.66% with FP16 attention and 2-bit experts, 65.58% with 4-bit attention and 2-bit experts (right-hand 3-bit/2-bit attention block: 61.83%, 55.26%).
transfers_to_us: Partly. It is the origin of 'quantize experts to 2 bits + LRU', but the offload tier is host RAM over PCIe on a GPU, k experts per layer cached out of 8, and Mixtral has only 8 big experts. Quality cost at 2-bit is visible (about -4 MMLU points even with FP16 attention).
caveat: Mixtral only; 2-bit experts are in the 'chosen' configurations; no disk tier; gains vs naive offloading, not against a bigger-cache 4-bit path at the same RAM.
notes: The comparison 'same RAM, fewer bits' is not isolated in the paper; that equal-RAM comparison is exactly what our byte-capacity simulation does.

title: HOBBIT: A Mixed Precision Expert Offloading System for Fast MoE Inference (Tang, Liu, Hou, Pu, Wang, Heng, Li, Guo; SJTU / CUHK; arXiv 2411.01433 v2, 6 Nov 2024)
setting: Built on llama.cpp (about 8,000 lines C++). Mixtral-8x7B and Phi-MoE (45B/42B, top-2). RTX 4090 24 GB (256 GB RAM, PCIe 4.0) with float16 + int4 replacements, and Jetson AGX Orin 32 GB unified memory with int8 + int2 replacements, model on Samsung 980 PRO NVMe (about 3 GB/s in practice); batch 1; Alpaca prompts. Baselines include llama.cpp (mmap), MoE-Infinity, MoE-Offloading, Transformers, DeepSpeed, Fiddler.
headline: Abstract: up to 9.93x decode vs SOTA offloading systems. Text: on Jetson Orin, 3.64x (Mixtral) and 9.93x (Phi-MoE) average decode speedup vs MoE-Infinity, and 13.0x / 18.9x vs llama.cpp (79-80% lower prefill latency). Table 3: GSM8K 0.52 -> 0.51 (Mixtral float16 vs float16+int4), 0.52 -> 0.51 (int8 vs int8+int2); Phi-MoE 0.83 -> 0.82 / 0.83.
transfers_to_us: Partly, closest on hardware class (NVMe + llama.cpp + batch 1) but: the low-precision copy is only used for low-importance cache-MISS experts (hot experts stay high-precision), which is a different idea from storing all experts at 2-3 bits; the Jetson baselines are llama.cpp mmap page-faulting and a GPU-server system, so 9.93x/13x measures a weak baseline.
caveat: Only two 42-45B models with 8-16 big experts; int2 replacement is applied only under an importance threshold; extra storage for multi-precision copies.
notes: Accuracy loss reported to be about 1 point, but only when a minority of loaded experts are swapped.

title: MoE-SpeQ (v1, 18 Nov 2025) renamed Specter: Fast MoE Inference via Quantization-Enabled Multi-Step Speculative Offloading in v3 (Wang, Hou, Xia, Wang, Zhang, Tang, Liu, Li; SJTU; arXiv 2511.14102 v3, 22 Oct 2026; ASPLOS '27)
setting: v3: Phi-3.5-MoE, Qwen1.5-MoE, DeepSeekV2-Lite, one NVIDIA A100 40 GB with 24-core Xeon, quantized (INT4) draft model on the GPU predicts future experts for multi-step PCIe prefetch; baselines include SpecMoEOff, Mixtral-Offloading-SC/SM, vLLM, Transformers, llama.cpp.
headline: v1 abstract: 'at most 2.34x' over the SOTA offloading framework on Phi-MoE. v3 abstract: average 1.50x (up to 1.88x) TPOT speedup over the SOTA speculative-offloading baseline; e.g. Phi-3.5-MoE TPOT 163.3 ms vs 292.1 ms SpecMoEOff, up to 5.9x vs Transformers. A search snippet quoting 3.3x (536.7 -> 163.1 ms) matches the 163 ms figure but I did not find it in the text I read.
transfers_to_us: No. The quantization here is of the DRAFT model (for routing prediction), not of the stored experts, so it does not support the 'requantize the experts' claim of #7; A100, PCIe.
caveat: Headline numbers changed between versions (2.34x -> 1.50x avg, different baseline); the catalog uses the superseded v1 numbers.

title: Making Every Verified Token Count: Adaptive Verification for MoE Speculative Decoding, EVICT (Pan, Tao, Wang, Zhao, Wang, Zhang; USTC; arXiv 2605.00342 v2, 5 Sep 2026)

README itself says gains need an I/O-bound regime, only help with explicit reads (mmap parity), shrink with LRU caching and large slices. Self-reported, 8 stars, one machine, 33 GB model on a machine with more RAM (squeezed).
notes: Closest published work to the family and uses a 512-expert model like ours. README also cites an independent MLX cross-check (+9.7% to +32% decode, 1.29-2.34x I/O) not verified by us. Layout trained on general data gave 1.22x on code (cross-domain transfer reported).

notes: Abstract only.

title: Building py-kvcache: A Performance Characterization of External KV Caching for vLLM with NVMe SSDs (Kanichai, De Matteis, Trivedi; arXiv 2609.11744, 10 Sep 2026)
setting: vLLM with GPU/CPU/NVMe tiers; H100 and a weaker GPU; LongBench, SCBench, Bailian traces
headline: 80k tokens: disk load 2.0x faster than LMCache, preloading 1.34x; 1.23x vs LMCache with all tiers, within ~4% of native vLLM offload; on H100 average request falls below break-even
caveat: Catalog's 'for our model prefill is slow so loading wins' is the catalog's inference, not the paper's; the paper's lesson is that a load-vs-recompute admission decision is setup-specific. For a 69 GB model prefill is I/O-bound so loading likely wins, but that is our arithmetic.
notes: Abstract only.

title: On 10X Better Scalability: KV Stores Scale Up KV Cache (SGLang-LSM; Yu, Ye, He, Liu, Luo; arXiv 2511.16138v2, 25 Nov 2025)
setting: GLM-4-8B, GLM-4-32B, Llama-3-8B; Xeon 4314, 64 GB RAM, A30 24 GB, 8 TB SSD; baseline SGLang file backend
headline: Hit rate up to +143% (4k prompts 45.4% vs 18.7%); TTFT -24% (16k: 1.78 s vs 2.35 s); 13-24% across models; Llama-3-8B KV 120 KB/token (GLM-4-8B 40, GLM-4-32B 60)
caveat: Server workload with LSM-tree prefix index on GPU box; gains are over another disk cache, not over no cache; figures only, no tables.

title: ProMoE: Fast MoE-based LLM Serving using Proactive Caching (Song, Zhong, Chen, Chen; arXiv 2410.22134, v1 29 Oct 2024, v3 1 Sep 2025; no venue on page)
setting: DeepSeek-moe, DeepSeek-V2-Lite, Qwen1.5-moe (FP16), Qwen2-moe, Mixtral (INT4); RTX 4090 24 GB + i9-14900K + 128 GB host DRAM over PCIe 4.0; batch 1; baselines transformers offload/LRU/static and llama.cpp
headline: Abstract: decode 2.07x avg (up to 5.02x) vs offloading baselines; text: llama.cpp decode 1.66x avg (up to 2.07x) vs LO/static/LRU, but only 1.09x (max 1.17x) vs LRU and 1.49x vs static; learned per-layer MLP predictor accuracy 84.7% (token-based 58.3%); lossless
caveat: Experts live in host DRAM and move over PCIe to a 24 GB GPU, not from NVMe; vs an LRU cache in llama.cpp decode gain is 1.09x; Mixtral decode is an exception (LO faster). The catalog's 1.66x/2.07x labels are swapped relative to the text vs abstract.
notes: Catalog url (alphaxiv) not used; arxiv abs and html opened.

title: HOBBIT: A Mixed Precision Expert Offloading System for Fast MoE Inference (Tang et al.; arXiv 2411.01433v2, 6 Nov 2024; no venue on page)
setting: Mixtral-8x7B (top-2 of 8), Phi-MoE (top-2 of 16); RTX 4090 + 256 GB RAM; Jetson AGX Orin 32 GB; Samsung 980 PRO NVMe; batch 1; built on llama.cpp (~8k lines)
headline: 9.93x avg decode (Phi-MoE vs MoE-Infinity on Orin, Int8 base + Int2 replacement experts); accuracy drop <=1% (GSM8K, TruthfulQA); next-layer top-1 prediction ~96% on Mixtral
caveat: Of the few papers with llama.cpp + NVMe + batch 1. But 9.93x is vs a GPU-oriented baseline, uses lossy low-precision substitution, and top-2-of-8 routing makes prediction and caching far easier than top-10-of-512.

title: Budgeting Bytes: A Windowed Storage Roofline and Dual-Budget Architecture Ablations for Storage-Bound LLM Decoding (Hanhaodi Zhang, single author; arXiv 2609.04238v1, 29 Jul 2026; workshop draft)
setting: Sub-100M-param ablations; Qwen3-30B-A3B 4-bit (18 GB) on an 8 GB edge board with eMMC; A100 PCIe offload; 16 GB unified-memory device
headline: Abstract: expert prefetching did not help on the 8 GB eMMC board, even with a perfect-prediction oracle; pre-attention probe predicts Qwen3-30B routing at 91.2%; it only converts to throughput when the fast tier holds most of the model; fitting the model gave 11.5 tok/s (22x)
caveat: The '18.8% previous-token hit on top-2-of-8' and 'madvise(WILLNEED) for llama.cpp' are not on the abstract page - unverified. Single-run configurations, single author.
notes: Abstract only; full text not read.

title: Pre-Attention Expert Prediction and Prefetching for MoE LLMs (Zhu, Bohl, Oester, Alonso; ETH; arXiv 2511.10676v1, 10 Nov 2025) and Speculating Experts Accelerates Inference for MoE (Madan, Singhania, Bhatele, Goldstein, Panda; arXiv 2603.19289, 9 Mar 2026)
setting: Paper 1: DeepSeek-V2-Lite, Qwen3-30B-A3B, Phi-mini-MoE; TITAN RTX, V100/A100 loading benchmarks. Paper 2: CPU-GPU expert offload, models/hardware not on page
headline: Paper 1: exact-match 93.03 / 94.69 / 97.62% (Arch 1), 92.31 / 91.82 / 96.63% (Arch 2); no end-to-end speedup, estimated 0.27-0.64 ms/token saved; loading 6 experts 33.5-49.8 ms from disk vs 4.0-9.5 ms from memory. Paper 2: up to 14% TPOT reduction vs on-demand CPU loading
caveat: Accuracy is high (same-layer predictor on pre-attention hidden state), but the gain it converts to is small: 14% TPOT in paper 2 and a loading-time estimate in paper 1; neither is NVMe-bound with a 2-8 footprint cache. Short lead (one layer) bounds benefit.
notes: Catalog merges two papers in one row; both opened (abstract + html for first).

title: Delta Decompression for MoE-based LLMs Compression (D2-MoE; Gu, Li, Li, Zhu, Lee, Sun, Xue, Guo; arXiv 2502.17298, 24 Feb 2025; ICML 2025 per search listing)
setting: Mixtral-8x7B, DeepSeekMoE-16B, Phi-3.5-MoE, Qwen2-57B-A14B; A100; 512 WikiText-2 calibration samples; training-free
headline: Mixtral WikiText-2 PPL 3.98 -> 4.65 / 5.28 / 6.46 at 20/40/60%, avg acc 0.63 -> 0.60 / 0.57 / 0.52; throughput at batch 64 (60%: 277.7 tok/s vs NAEE 271.9, MoE-I2 227.6); no uncompressed throughput given
caveat: Compresses by dropping shared-base and delta rank (lossy, 40-60% size), tested on GPU at batch 64; no offloading or disk setting; quality costs are real (acc 0.63 -> 0.57 at 40%).

title: MoBE: Mixture-of-Basis-Experts for Compressing MoE-based LLMs (Chen, Ha, Lan, Zhang, Li; arXiv 2508.05257, 7 Aug 2025)
setting: Qwen3-30B-A3B-2507, Qwen3-235B-A22B-2507, DeepSeek-V3-0324, Kimi-K2, Ling-Lite, DS-V2-Lite; H100; Adam optimisation, no distillation
headline: Params -24-30% on the three large models, 1-2% absolute accuracy drop (retention ~96-99% over 15 benchmarks; Qwen3-30B 24% -> 78.6 to 75.8); no speed numbers
caveat: Only gate/up compressed; fitting is a trained optimisation (not training-free); extra per-expert matrices can raise active parameters; authors say no throughput results and need a custom kernel; 24-30% is ~1.3-1.4x bytes, far from 3x.
notes: Authors argue expert matrices have effective rank above SVD thresholds, consistent with our flat spectrum (OLMoE probe).

title: MoE-SVD: Structured Mixture-of-Experts LLMs Compression via Singular Value Decomposition (Li, Li, Gu, Huang, Lee, Sun, Xue, Guo; ICML 2025 poster)
setting: Mixtral, Phi-3.5, DeepSeek, Qwen2 MoE; hardware not on page
headline: 60% compression, 1.5x faster inference, training-free (abstract)
caveat: Abstract only; speedup is GPU compute-bound inference, not expert streaming; quality tables not read.
notes: Hardware and tables unverified.

title: DeltaMoE: Memory-Efficient Inference for Merged Mixture of Experts with Delta Compression (Borisov, Yao, Gurel, Klimovic; ICLR 2025 SLLM workshop)
setting: Merged SMoE models (built by merging fine-tuned models); hardware/baseline not on abstract page
headline: Up to 2.34x compression, up to 2.57x throughput (abstract)
caveat: Deltas are relative to a base in merged/fine-tuned models, whose experts are close to a shared base by construction; pretrained MoE experts are not. Workshop paper, abstract only, setup unverified.

title: Bandwidth-Efficient Adaptive Mixture-of-Experts via Low-Rank Compensation (Liu et al.; arXiv 2512.17073, 18 Dec 2025)
setting: Mixtral-8x7B, 8x22B, DeepSeek-MoE-16B; H100 over PCIe from DDR, plus simulated GPU-NDP; INT3/INT2 experts, INT3 compensators; baselines Mixtral-Offloading (FP16), HOBBIT, MoNDE
headline: Mixtral-8x7B 2.37 -> 12.27 (3-bit) / 18.11 (2-bit) tok/s vs Mixtral-Offloading; vs HOBBIT 6.75 -> 25.43 / 36.97; uniform GPTQ INT2 avg accuracy 70.03% -> 34.41%; compensator rank 16 = 0.32 MB (0.75% of an INT2 expert)
caveat: Baseline is FP16 PCIe offloading (so 5-8x is mostly just fewer bytes); GPU/simulated NDP; batch size unspecified; shows INT2 alone collapses accuracy and a small per-expert low-rank fix on top-n experts recovers much of it, which is relevant to our '2-bit base + residual for top experts' variant (family 9), not to a shared-basis scheme.
notes: Catalog says 'low-rank compensator offsets low-bit error' - correct; it is per-expert, not shared across experts.

title: Dr.LLM: Dynamic Layer Routing in LLMs (Heakl, Gubri, Khan, Yun, Oh; arXiv 2510.12773, 14 Oct 2025, page says 'Under submission'; catalog says ICLR 2026, not confirmed on page)
setting: Dense LLaMA-3.2/3.1 3B and 8B (Instruct and Base) and Qwen-2.5 3B/7B; one A100 40GB; routers ~11M params (3B) / 16.8M (8B) trained on 4k MCTS-labelled examples (ARC, DART-Math); baselines vanilla model, LayerSkip, ShortGPT, MindSkip, FlexiDepth (FlexiDepth numbers copied from its paper, LLaMA-8B only)
headline: Table 3: accuracy +0.9..+3.2 points in-domain with 3.0-8.7 fewer layers per example; Table 4: 0.85 point average out-of-domain drop over 8 benchmarks; 1000-token generation 29.21 s vs 34.49 s (15.3% less); batch-1 throughput +26.89% on LLaMA-3B-Instruct, batch average +8.65% (Table 7)
caveat: Skips only ~10-15% of layers on dense 3-8B models, GPU, per-layer batch sync; no MoE model, no disk-bound regime; routing F1 only 61% macro; abstract/body inconsistent on layers saved (5 vs up to 11); out-of-domain drops up to ~4.8 points on single tasks
notes: Skipped layer in a streamed-expert model would also skip that layer's expert reads, which the paper does not study. Our arithmetic (25% skip -> 1.33x) is consistent with their scale of gain.

title: LayerSkip: Enabling Early Exit Inference and Self-Speculative Decoding (Elhoushi et al., Meta, ACL 2024; arXiv 2404.16710)
setting: Llama models of unstated sizes (abstract only); hardware not stated on page; requires special training recipe (layer dropout + early-exit loss with shared exit)
headline: Up to 2.16x CNN/DM, 1.82x coding, 2.0x TOPv2 (abstract); only abstract pages opened, tables not seen
caveat: Speedup comes from draft-and-verify (self-speculative decoding), lossless; needs the model pre/continually trained with the recipe; for a sparse MoE the verify pass would touch more experts per step so streaming cost can go up not down
notes: Results tables not read; speedup numbers are 'up to' on dense Llama. Unverified beyond abstract.

title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect (Men et al.; arXiv 2403.03853, v1 6 Mar 2024, v3 11 Oct 2024)
setting: Llama2-7B/13B, Baichuan2-7B/13B (also RWKV-7B, Mamba-2.8B); hardware not stated; training-free pruning by Block Influence; Llama2-13B removes layers 26-35 (10 of 40)
headline: Intro: Llama2-13B MMLU 55.0 -> 52.2 after removing 10 layers; Table 2 instead gives 54.69 vs 55.00 at 24.6% removed (internal inconsistency); Table 4: GPTQ Llama2-7B throughput 1.00x -> ~1.16x at 25% layers removed
caveat: Dense models only; generative tasks (XSum, C3) collapse to near zero when 25% of layers are removed on the 7B models; the 13B holds up better; speedup is only 1.16x at 25% removal; no MoE
notes: Intro and Table 2 MMLU numbers disagree, so the catalog's 55.0->52.2 is the intro figure.

title: The Diminishing Returns of Early-Exit Decoding in Modern LLMs (Wei, Du, Yu, Tiwari, Li, Xu, Wang; arXiv 2603.23701, 24 Mar 2026); catalog points at an alphaXiv overview of it
setting: Models include Llama2/3/4-Scout, Qwen2/3 incl. Qwen3-30B-A3B, GPT-OSS-20B, Mamba; hardware not reported; analysis of early-exit potential (EAS metric), no latency measured
headline: Overview page: MMLU Llama2-7B 0.41->0.38 skipping 4.69% of layers; Llama3-8B 0.54->0.52 skipping 0.18%. Full paper: GPT-OSS-20B EAS 0.59 (highest, Table 3), Llama4-Scout 0.47; MoE models argued to defer decisions to deeper layers, but no numeric EAS for Qwen3-30B-A3B in text
caveat: The overview page names no MoE result; only the full paper has the MoE claim, and it is partly contradicted by its own Table 3 (GPT-OSS-20B has the highest EAS). Oracle early exit within 5% accuracy loss skips only ~4.5-7.3% of layers on GPT-OSS-20B
notes: Catalog calls it 'Early-exit analysis for MoE models'; the paper is not MoE-specific and the catalog's 'secondary, numbers unverified' flag was right. I opened the primary arXiv HTML (first 100k chars).

title: MoE-Infinity: Efficient MoE Inference on Personal Machines with Sparsity-Aware Expert Cache (Xue, Fu, Lu, Mai, Marina; arXiv 2401.14361 v3, 12 Mar 2025)
setting: One RTX A5000 24GB over PCIe 4.0, weights fully in host RAM (32-1024 GB); Switch, DeepSeek-V2-Lite, NLLB-MoE, Mixtral-8x7B, Arctic; batch 1, prompt 512, decode 32; baselines DeepSpeed, Ollama(llama.cpp), Mixtral-Offloading, BrainStorm (own reimplementation), vLLM
headline: Abstract 3.1-16.7x lower per-token latency (conclusion says 2.7-13.7x). Table 1 DeepSeek-V2-Lite TPOT avg: MoE-Infinity 155 ms vs vLLM 485, DeepSpeed 737, Mixtral-Offloading 1250, Ollama 2590. Mixtral worst case ~836 ms, only 1.4x over Mixtral-Offloading
caveat: Experts come from host RAM over PCIe to a GPU, not from NVMe to CPU; method is request-level activation-matrix matching (cosine) for prefetch and eviction, not a static frequency pin; gain is against weak baselines; on Mixtral (closest to a big-expert model) only 1.4x over a LRU+prefetch system
notes: Abstract vs conclusion range inconsistent. Our static-frequency-pin analogue is not the paper's algorithm.

title: KBVQ-MoE: KLT-guided SVD with Bias-Corrected Vector Quantization for MoE LLMs (Xu, Zhao, Hu, Chen, Yang; arXiv 2602.11184 v2, Feb 2026; ICLR 2026 poster confirmed by search result)
setting: Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B and Qwen3-30B-A3B (others); RTX A6000; VQ vector length 4, SVD rank 1/128; baselines RTN, GPTQ, MoEQuant, plain VQ; calibration 256 RedPajama samples
headline: Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B: FP16 PPL 7.22 / avg acc 68.07; 3-bit KBVQ 7.74 / 67.99; 2-bit KBVQ 9.61 / 62.78 vs plain VQ 11.47 / 55.94 and GPTQ 2-bit 7.58 / 66.36. 2.08 effective bits; decoder speed 35.24 vs 22.31 tok/s BF16 (1.58x, hardware unstated)
caveat: At 2-bit its own table shows GPTQ and MoEQuant beating it on this model; uses 4-dim vectors and 2.08 bits, not 8-dim at 1.3 bpw; quality at 1.3 bpw not shown; speed is GPU BF16 comparison with unnamed kernels
notes: Reads as evidence that plain VQ degrades (acc 55.94) and needs shared components plus bias correction, matching our k-means probe.

title: QMoE: Practical Sub-1-Bit Compression of Trillion-Parameter Models (Frantar, Alistarh; arXiv 2310.16795, 25 Oct 2023)
setting: SwitchTransformer-c2048 (1.6T) only; compression on 1 A6000, inference on 4xA6000 or 8x3090; baselines RTN and BF16
headline: 0.807 bits/param, ~19.8x, under 160 GB; C4 validation loss 1.26 ternary vs 1.18 BF16 (RTN ternary 2.15); <5% end-to-end overhead vs uncompressed (own estimate); kernels up to 35% faster than BF16 on some shapes
caveat: Switch models are extremely redundant (2048 experts, encoder-decoder, T5-style); custom GPU kernel decodes 16-bit dictionary codewords; mixtral-offloading authors report sub-1-bit QMoE gave too much perplexity loss on Mixtral; no CPU path
notes: Only C4 loss reported, not zero-shot accuracy.

title: Mixture of Quantized Experts (MoQE): Complementary Effect of Low-bit Quantization and Robustness (Kim, Fahim, Awadalla; arXiv 2310.02410, 3 Oct 2023)
setting: Machine-translation MoE (5.3B params, 32 experts; WMT-10 128-expert variant), not an LLM; one A100; dense fp16 BLEU 45.06, MoE fp16 46.35
headline: Table 2 avg BLEU: int8 46.34, int4 46.18 (1.24x throughput, 0.32x size), int3 46.01, int2 with QAT 45.90 (0.20x size). 79.6% size cut is the int2 figure. Table 5 public WMT 2-bit drops ~11-12 BLEU
caveat: The headline int2 result is with quantization-aware training; post-training 2-bit drops 1.82 BLEU in one setting and ~12 BLEU in another; MT models with 32-128 small experts, not a decoder LLM; no optimized kernel below 4-bit; speedup is 4-bit on A100
notes: Catalog one-liner omits QAT. The qualitative claim (experts tolerate low bits better than dense FFN, outlier skewness Table 3) is supported.

title: Fast Inference of Mixture-of-Experts Language Models with Offloading (Eliseev, Mazur; arXiv 2312.17238) and repo dvmazur/mixtral-offloading
setting: Mixtral-8x7B; attention 4-bit HQQ, experts 2- or 3-bit; T4 (Colab), RTX 3060, RTX 3080 Mobile, A100 (reference); LRU cache k=2 (3060) or k=4; batch 1
headline: Table 2 2-bit tok/s full algorithm: A100 3.061, 3080M 2.655, 3060 2.278, T4 2.092; naive offloading 0.66-1.39; ablation: no LRU/pre-load 1.17-2.27. Table 1 MMLU 70.51 FP16, 70.3 4/4-bit, 66.66 for 4-bit attn + 2-bit experts (19.33 GB); 2-bit averages ~2.6 bits incl. scales
caveat: GPU with experts in host RAM over PCIe, not NVMe on CPU; 8 large experts per layer (our 512 small experts differ); speeds dominated by PCIe bandwidth
notes: Repo page itself has no numbers; they are in the paper. A 3.85 point MMLU drop at 2-bit experts is the quality cost in a coarse-grained MoE.

title: VPTQ: Extreme Low-bit Vector Post-Training Quantization for LLMs (Microsoft; EMNLP 2024); catalog URL is the PyPI page
setting: PyPI page failed to load (site error); content verified from github.com/microsoft/VPTQ (archived): Llama 2/3.x, Qwen 2.5, Mistral Large, DeepSeek R1 (preliminary); CUDA/ROCm
headline: GitHub README tech-report values: LLaMA-2 7B ~2.0-2.3 bits W2 PPL 6.13-5.95, ~36-40 tok/s; 70B ~2.1 bits ~9.7 tok/s; 70B at ~2 bits on RTX 4090. Roadmap lists contributing to llama.cpp/exllama as planned
caveat: Roadmap item for llama.cpp is not delivered, repo is archived and 'research only'; GPU kernels; dense models mostly
notes: PyPI url unverified; GitHub README used instead and says the same on llama.cpp.

title: GPTVQ: The Blessing of Dimensionality for LLM Quantization (van Baalen et al., Qualcomm; arXiv 2402.15319, v1 23 Feb 2024, v2 3 Jun 2025)
setting: Llama-v2 and Mistral; H100 for quantization (Llama-v2-70B 3-11 h); mobile-CPU timings for VQ decode; abstract page only
headline: Abstract: new state of the art in size-vs-accuracy; VQ shows better latency than a 4-bit integer format on a mobile CPU. No perplexity numbers on the page
caveat: Tables not seen (abstract only), so '2 to 3 bits' numbers unverified; dense models; Hessian-based, needs calibration; the mobile CPU latency claim is the one useful for a CPU-only setting
notes: Closest published evidence that VQ decode can be cheap on CPU; read the full tables before relying.

title: Mixture Compressor for Mixture-of-Experts LLMs Gains More (Huang et al.; arXiv 2410.06270 v2, 22 Feb 2025)
setting: Mixtral-8x7B (main) and 8x22B; compression on 2-4 A100-80GB, tested on A100 and one RTX 3090; baselines uniform GPTQ 2/3-bit, BSP, HAWQ-style
headline: Mixtral 8x7B 16-bit avg 71.29; PMQ 2.54-bit 67.50 (96.8 -> 16.24 GB); +ODP 66.94; 2.05-bit 63.25 (62.68 with ODP, 1.80x speedup); 1.57-bit 54.49; uniform 2-bit GPTQ 42.67; GSM8K 58.30 -> 37.67 and HumanEval 59.15 -> 29.34 at 2.54-bit
caveat: Only Mixtral (8 experts); heavy damage on reasoning/code at 2.5 bits; speedups use a custom CUDA kernel and 2-GPU vs 1-GPU comparison
notes: Bit allocation scores experts by activation frequency, routing weight and reconstruction error; the 'hotness-driven' idea of family #9 already appears here.

title: D2MoE: Dual Routing and Dynamic Scheduling for Efficient On-Device MoE-based LLM Serving (Wang, Zhou, Hong, Guo; arXiv 2504.15299; ACM MobiCom '25)
setting: LLaMA-MoE-3.5B and Mixtral-8x7B; RTX 3060 6GB + i7-11800H + 32 GB RAM + 970 EVO SSD (3.5 GB/s) and Jetson AGX Orin 64GB; baselines Hold-in-Memory INT8/AWQ, GPTQ multi-version, EdgeMoE, MoQE-DynaIO; concurrency 4-32 requests
headline: Up to 1.39x throughput vs latest on-device frameworks (Mixtral 1.14-1.39x vs EdgeMoE; 1.42-3.37x vs MoQE-DynaIO), up to 53% lower peak memory; WikiText2 PPL Mixtral 4.09 vs 4.04 (INT8), LLaMA-MoE 14.58 vs 14.55; dequant overhead 5-20%, router 1-2%
caveat: Nested ladders are INT2->4 (V1) and INT5->8 (V2) with per-token bit-width router fine-tuned 2-4 h; GPU-assisted (RTX 3060) with SSD loads; multi-request concurrency; 8 big experts; gain over the strongest baseline only 1.14-1.39x
notes: Uses 'hottest-expert-bit-first' I/O scheduling; its SSD+RAM setting is the closest published one to ours among #9 rows, but GPU-assisted.

title: Catalog URL is MatGPTQ: Efficient and Accurate Inference over Nested Quantized Models (Kleinegger, Crnčević, Alistarh; arXiv 2602.03537, v1 3 Feb 2026, v2 30 Sep 2026); the Matryoshka Quantization original is Nair et al., ICML 2025, arXiv 2502.06786
setting: MatGPTQ: Llama3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B on RTX A6000; dense only, no MoE; baselines GPTQ, own MatQuant reimplementation, Any-Precision-LLM, AnyBCQ. MatQuant: known only from search snippets (not opened)
headline: MatGPTQ: accuracy reported at 3, 4, 6, 8 bit (no int2 accuracy); kernels 2x-6.5x over FP16 cuBLAS memory-bound, end-to-end 2.8-3.9x (HF), 1.7-3.5x (vLLM); falls behind Marlin from batch 16. MatQuant (snippet): int2 gains up to 4% (OmniQuant) / 7% (QAT) over standard int2; abstract v1 claimed 10%
caveat: The catalog's 'int2-in-int4-in-int8' describes MatQuant, but the URL opened is MatGPTQ, which does not report int2 accuracy and never touches MoE; GPU kernels; speedups vs BF16 weights, not vs a 4-bit CPU path
notes: Two papers conflated. MatQuant itself unverified (search snippets only).

title: Catalog URL is GEMQ: Global Expert-Level Mixed-Precision Quantization for MoE LLMs (Deng et al.; arXiv 2605.23078, 21 May 2026); DynaExq is a different paper, arXiv 2511.15015 (Chu et al., v1 19 Nov 2025, v4 10 Sep 2026)
setting: GEMQ (alphaXiv summary page): DeepSeekV2-Lite, Qwen1.5-MoE, Mixtral-8x7B; one H100 80GB; baseline PMQ. DynaExq (arXiv abstract + search summary): Qwen3-30B and Qwen3-80B on a single memory-limited GPU, batch size 32
headline: GEMQ Mixtral 2.5 bit/expert: 65.13% 0-shot avg vs PMQ 64.34%; 87 GB -> 'roughly 18 GB'; 82.5 tok/s on H100; DeepSeekV2-Lite 6.1x memory and 1.6x speed. DynaExq: Qwen3-80B accuracy 73.09 -> 77.57 over static PTQ, up to 2.73x throughput vs offloading at batch 32
caveat: The catalog's '16 GB' and '7% MMLU drop' are not on the page (it says ~18 GB and gives no MMLU); DynaExq is a GPU HBM-budget design at batch 32, GEMQ is a static allocation
notes: Catalog merges two papers under one URL; numbers for GEMQ do not match what the page shows. Page is a third-party summary and v1, so unverified against the paper itself.

title: Exploiting Inter-Layer Expert Affinity for Accelerating MoE Model Inference (ExFlow)
setting: GPT MoE 350M-1.3B top-1, A100 NVLink+IB
